title: Beginner Spanish
summary: Start speaking Spanish: greetings and introductions, tú and usted, pronunciation and numbers, nouns, gender and articles, ser and estar, regular present-tense verbs, questions and negation, and everyday phrases for family, food and time.
audience: Complete beginners, students, travellers and professionals working with Spanish speakers

body.p: Spanish is spoken as a first language by hundreds of millions of people across Spain, Latin America and Equatorial Guinea, where it is an official language, and it is one of the most studied languages in the world. It opens doors to travel, business, literature and international organisations.

list: Hola: hello.
Buenos días: good morning. Buenas tardes: good afternoon. Buenas noches: good evening, good night.
¿Cómo estás? (informal) / ¿Cómo está usted? (formal): How are you?
Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?: Fine, thanks. And you?
Me llamo Wanjiru: My name is Wanjiru.
¿Cómo te llamas?: What is your name?
Mucho gusto: pleased to meet you.
Adiós: goodbye. Hasta luego: see you later.
Por favor: please. Gracias: thank you. De nada: you're welcome. Perdón / Disculpe: excuse me.

body.p: Use tú with friends, family and peers, and usted with strangers, elders and in formal situations. In Spain, vosotros is the informal plural "you"; in Latin America, ustedes is used for all plural "you".

body.tip: Notice the upside-down question and exclamation marks at the start of sentences: ¿…? and ¡…!. They are part of correct Spanish writing.

body.p: Spanish spelling is very regular: once you know the rules, you can pronounce almost any word you read.

list: Five pure vowels: a (as in "father"), e (as in "bed"), i (as in "machine"), o (as in "more"), u (as in "food").
h is silent: hola sounds like "ola".
j sounds like a strong "h": José.
ñ sounds like "ny": mañana (tomorrow), España.
ll is usually like "y": llamar.
rr is a rolled r: perro (dog); a single r between vowels is a quick tap: pero (but).
Stress: words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-last syllable; others on the last; written accents mark exceptions: café, inglés.

body.p: 1 uno, 2 dos, 3 tres, 4 cuatro, 5 cinco, 6 seis, 7 siete, 8 ocho, 9 nueve, 10 diez, 11 once, 12 doce, 13 trece, 14 catorce, 15 quince, 16 dieciséis, 17 diecisiete, 18 dieciocho, 19 diecinueve, 20 veinte, 30 treinta, 40 cuarenta, 50 cincuenta, 100 cien.

body.tip: Read Spanish words aloud slowly, vowel by vowel; accurate vowels make you easy to understand.

body.p: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine. Many masculine nouns end in -o and many feminine nouns in -a, but there are exceptions (el día, la mano), so learn each noun with its article.

list: Definite (the): el (masculine), la (feminine), los (masculine plural), las (feminine plural): el libro, la casa, los libros, las casas.
Indefinite (a, some): un, una, unos, unas: un amigo, una amiga.
Plurals: add -s after a vowel (casa, casas) and -es after a consonant (ciudad, ciudades).

body.p: Adjectives agree in gender and number and usually follow the noun: un coche rojo (a red car), una casa blanca (a white house), los niños altos (the tall boys). Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant often have one form for both genders: una chica inteligente, un chico inteligente.

body.tip: When you learn a noun, say it with its article and an adjective: la casa grande. It trains gender agreement automatically.

list: Ser for identity, origin, profession and lasting characteristics: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. Soy keniana (I am Kenyan). Ella es profesora (She is a teacher).
Estar for location, temporary states and feelings: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están. Estoy cansado (I am tired). La escuela está cerca (The school is nearby).

body.p: Verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir. Remove the ending and add endings for each person. Hablar (to speak): hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. Comer (to eat): como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen. Vivir (to live): vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.
Subject pronouns (yo, tú, él, ella, nosotros, vosotros, ellos, ellas, usted, ustedes) are often left out because the ending shows who is acting: Hablo español (I speak Spanish).
tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. Tener is used for age: Tengo veinte años (I am twenty years old), and in expressions such as tengo hambre (I am hungry).

body.tip: Ask yourself "permanent identity or current state?" to choose between ser and estar.

list: Rising intonation with question marks: ¿Hablas inglés? (Do you speak English?)
Question words carry accents: ¿Qué? (what), ¿Quién? (who), ¿Dónde? (where), ¿Cuándo? (when), ¿Por qué? (why), ¿Cómo? (how), ¿Cuánto? (how much).
Examples: ¿Dónde vives? (Where do you live?) ¿Cuánto cuesta? (How much does it cost?) ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?)

body.p: Put no before the verb: Hablo francés → No hablo francés (I don't speak French). Double negatives are correct in Spanish: No tengo nada (I have nothing; literally "I don't have nothing"). Porque (one word, no accent) means "because": ¿Por qué estudias? Porque quiero viajar (Why do you study? Because I want to travel).

body.tip: Learn "¿Puede repetir, por favor?" (Can you repeat, please?) and "No entiendo" (I don't understand); they keep conversations going.

lessons.title: Everyday Spanish: family, food and time

body.p: la madre (mother), el padre (father), el hermano (brother), la hermana (sister), los padres (parents), el hijo / la hija (son / daughter), los abuelos (grandparents). Possessives: mi padre, mis hermanos, tu madre.

list: Quiero… / Quisiera… : I want… / I would like… (more polite)
agua, café, té, pan, arroz, pollo, fruta (water, coffee, tea, bread, rice, chicken, fruit)
¿Cuánto cuesta? : How much is it?
La cuenta, por favor : The bill, please.

body.p: lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo (Monday to Sunday; not capitalised). ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?) Es la una (It's one o'clock). Son las tres (It's three o'clock). Son las cuatro y media (It's half past four).

body.tip: Watch short Spanish videos with Spanish subtitles; reading and hearing together speeds up learning.
